A higher lease kilometre allowance can have two cost crossovers: compare the payment and the excess rate

Follow two hypothetical lease-distance offers through allowance breakpoints, extra monthly payments, a return bill and changing annual-equivalent driving.

By TickerLantern Research · Published 25 October 2026 · 5 min read
Sources reviewed 25 October 2026

Change an assumption. Follow the result.

Compare distance-related costs above the lease charges common to both offers

Interactive planning lab

Option A distance-related cost above common lease charges$2,400
Option B extra payments plus excess-distance charge$900
Option B minus A; negative means B costs less in this comparison-$1,500

Original nominal-CAD comparison of two hypothetical full-term lease returns. The vehicle, term, starting odometer convention, initial cash and all other lease and running costs are assumed identical and omitted. Option B has the entered additional all-in payment at each month-end. Each annual-equivalent allowance is multiplied by whole lease years to form one total contract kilometre allowance; there is no annual reset, forfeiture or separate annual excess charge. Total actual driving equals the entered annual-equivalent distance times years. At return, only distance above each total allowance is charged at that option’s entered flat all-in CAD-per-km rate. No credit for unused allowance, refund of higher monthly payments, buyout, early termination, fee waiver, wear charge, tax calculation, discounting or saving-account interest is included. The model is not a manufacturer offer. At the selected use, total distance is 60,000 km, versus allowances of 48,000 km for A and 72,000 km for B. Annual-equivalent driving is a way to state the term total, not a probability or promise that use is uniform.

The central idea

The included kilometres, payment premium and excess-kilometre rate are separate terms. Compare them over the full return period before treating a larger allowance as cheaper.

01

Compare the distance terms while holding the rest of the offer constant

A lower monthly lease payment can come with fewer included kilometres. A larger allowance can cost more each month and still carry a different charge for driving beyond it. Comparing just one of those numbers can miss the point where the other offer becomes cheaper.

This guide compares two original hypothetical offers for the same vehicle and full return date. All initial cash, common monthly lease charges and other vehicle costs are assumed identical and omitted. The charts include only the extra monthly payment for option B and the excess-distance charges at return. They do not display the full lease or ownership cost.

Nissan Canada’s leasing glossary describes a kilometre allowance and an excess charge for going beyond the contractual limit, with that charge paid when the vehicle is returned. It provides context for the terms, not the prices or hypothetical offers used in this tool.

02

Translate the annual-equivalent allowance into the assumed contract total

The example lasts three whole years, or 36 months. Option A has an annual-equivalent allowance of 16,000 km, giving 48,000 km over the full term. Option B has 24,000 km per year in the same sense, giving a 72,000 km total.

The model tests one aggregate allowance at return. It does not charge excess distance separately at the end of each year, discard unused annual amounts or reset the odometer. “Annual equivalent” is a way to express the term total. Actual contract provisions must determine whether that is the correct interpretation for a real offer.

The selected annual-equivalent driving is 20,000 km, so total use is 60,000 km. That creates 12,000 excess kilometres under A and none under B. The arithmetic depends on total use over the term, not on whether those kilometres were driven evenly each year.

03

Separate the certain payment premium from the contingent return charge

Option B costs an additional CAD 25 per month, or CAD 900 over 36 months. The assumed all-in excess rates are CAD 0.20 per km for A and CAD 0.30 per km for B. These are independent authored quotes, not current rates from a manufacturer.

At 60,000 total kilometres, A’s charge is 12,000 × CAD 0.20 = CAD 2,400. B has no excess-distance charge but still pays its CAD 900 premium. B’s modeled distance-related cost is therefore CAD 1,500 lower at this use level.

The extra payment does not disappear when the larger allowance is unused. At low enough driving, A has no excess charge and B still has its payment premium. There is no refund for unused allowance in this illustration, and no assumed waiver of a charge because the customer takes another vehicle.

04

Locate the first crossover while B remains within its allowance

Between annual-equivalent driving of 16,000 and 24,000 km, only A has an excess-distance charge. Let k be annual-equivalent kilometres. A’s three-year charge is 3 × (k − 16,000) × CAD 0.20, while B’s distance-related cost remains CAD 900.

Setting them equal gives k = 16,000 + 900 ÷ 0.60, or 17,500 km per year. At that point, the two modeled distance costs are equal. Below it, A’s charge has not yet reached B’s premium; above it, B initially has the lower cost.

This is a threshold under the entered quotes. It is not a driving recommendation, a predicted odometer reading or proof that another vehicle’s offer has the same crossover. Changing the extra monthly payment, term or rate changes the comparison.

05

A different excess rate can create a second crossover

Above 24,000 annual-equivalent kilometres, both offers have excess charges. A’s cost rises by CAD 0.60 for each additional annual-equivalent kilometre over the three-year term. B’s rises by CAD 0.90, reflecting its higher assumed per-kilometre rate.

With the default inputs, the two expressions are A = 0.60k − 9,600 and B = 0.90k − 20,700. They meet again at 37,000 km per year, where both distance-related costs are CAD 12,600. B is cheaper between the two crossings, but A becomes cheaper again above the second one.

For example, at 40,000 km per year, A costs CAD 14,400 while B costs CAD 15,300, making B CAD 900 more expensive. Its larger included allowance has not vanished; the higher rate on the remaining excess distance eventually outweighs that advantage.

Now set B’s rate to CAD 0.20 per km. The higher-distance sections become parallel and that second crossover disappears. The tool does not assume that every pair of quotes must cross once, twice or at all.

06

Plan the final bill even when the total-cost comparison is clear

The cash calendar shows a different issue from which option has the lower total. In the selected 20,000-km example, A pays the modeled CAD 2,400 at return, while B’s CAD 900 leaves as CAD 25 monthly payments. The chart assumes the return bill is paid in the final month; an actual invoice date can differ.

If A’s projected charge remains CAD 2,400, setting aside CAD 66.67 per month for 36 months would approximately fund it without interest, allowing for cent rounding. A transfer to that reserve is not another vehicle expense: the expense is still the final charge. The reserve simply changes how cash is prepared.

Changing actual use changes the projected final bill. A job change, move or different commute therefore belongs in an updated term-distance estimate. A lower scheduled payment does not by itself mean the lower total cash commitment has been fully budgeted.

07

Read the actual return terms before using the comparison

  1. Put both offers on the same vehicle, term and initial-cash basis.
  2. Identify whether the kilometre allowance applies to the full contract or another period.
  3. Use each offer’s own excess rate and all-in payment difference.
  4. Test low, expected and higher use without assigning unsupported probabilities.
  5. Prepare for the return invoice separately from the regular payment.

The signed matrix changes annual-equivalent driving and B’s payment premium while preserving the selected allowances, rates and term. A negative cell means B costs less within this limited comparison; a positive cell means A costs less. The table retains exact calculated values.

Wear charges, damage, servicing, insurance, fuel, taxes beyond the entered all-in amounts, deposits, early termination, buyout and possible waivers are outside the model. If those terms differ between actual offers, they must be added before the distance-only result is treated as a full lease comparison.
